fixes.explanation: Peter writes, “Grace and peace be multiplied to you through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.” That's the wish he opens his letter with. Multiplied, friend. That's a big word to start with, and knowing God and Jesus is how he says it happens.

Peter doesn't mention the prayers of the apostles here. He says grace and peace are multiplied “…through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.” Peter calls himself an apostle in the first verse, and even he points to that knowledge. So the answer is knowing God and Jesus.
Peter never says to add to wealth. He says to make every effort “…to add to your faith virtue…” Faith is what they already have, and that's what he builds on. Wealth isn't in these verses, friend.

Peter says to add “to” each quality, not to trade one for another. Nobody swaps virtue out for knowledge. He writes “…and to knowledge, self-control…” and keeps going the same way. The list stacks, friend.
Every quality in Peter's list is added to the one before it. He writes “…and to knowledge, self-control…” so each one is tied to the last. None of them gets left off by itself, friend.

Peter says that if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, “…they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Notice the two parts of his if: having the qualities, and continuing to grow in them. Ineffective and unproductive are the two things he says they keep you from. I'm still working on the growing part myself, friend.

That one's True, friend. Peter writes that if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, “…they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The statement matches his words, so there's nothing hiding in it. Sometimes a True is just a True, and I can't blame you for squinting at it.

Peter writes, “For if you practice these things you will never stumble…” Never, friend. I trip over my own mustache on a good day, so I like hearing that word. The if in his sentence is practicing these things.

Peter doesn't say life gets easier. What he says is, “…if you practice these things you will never stumble…” That's the promise in his words. An easier life isn't what he names, and I can only tell you what Peter wrote, friend.

Peter writes, “…you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.” Lavish, friend. That's no sticker and a handshake at the door. He says it's waiting in the eternal kingdom of Jesus, and that's worth keeping the ovens ready for.

Quiet isn't Peter's word. A quiet entrance isn't what he describes. He says “…you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.” Lavish is the word on the page, friend.
